image.caption: Medea's murder of Apsyrtus, painted enamel plaque by Martin Didier Pape, c. 1580–1600 (Walters Art Museum)

versions.title: Izanagi Flees the Underworld
versions.teaser: A comb becomes bamboo shoots, a headdress becomes grapes.
versions.text:
Izanagi goes down to Yomi to bring back his dead wife, Izanami. She has already eaten the food of that land and asks him to wait while she consults its gods, and not to look at her. He waits, grows impatient, breaks a tooth off the comb in his hair, lights it, and looks. She is rotting, crawling with maggots, with eight thunder gods lodged in her body.

He runs. The hags of Yomi chase him. He throws down his black vine headdress, and it turns into wild grapes; while they stop to eat, he gains ground. Then he breaks the comb from the right side of his hair and throws it, and it sprouts bamboo shoots; they stop again to eat. The thunder gods follow with an army, and he fights them off with his sword swung behind him. At the pass between the worlds he throws three peaches, which drive them back. Finally he blocks the pass with a boulder, and husband and wife divorce across it.

versions.title: The Towel and the Comb
versions.teaser: A girl escaping Baba Yaga throws down a towel that becomes a river.
versions.text:
A stepmother sends her stepdaughter to her sister, who is Baba Yaga, to borrow a needle and thread. At Baba Yaga's hut she is set to weaving while the witch tells her servant to heat the bath and wash the girl well, for breakfast. The girl gives the servant a kerchief and asks her to go slowly; she gives the cat some ham, and the cat hands her a towel and a comb.

She runs. The dogs let her pass because she gives them bread, the gate because she oils its hinges, the birch tree because she ties it with a ribbon. Baba Yaga flies after her in her mortar. The girl throws the towel behind her, and it becomes a wide river. Baba Yaga brings her oxen to drink it dry. The girl throws the comb, and it becomes a dense forest that the witch cannot gnaw her way through. The girl gets home, her father learns the truth, and the stepmother gets what she deserves.

image.caption: Baba Yaga in her mortar, illustration by Ivan Bilibin, 1900

versions.title: The Battle of the Birds
versions.teaser: A giant's daughter flees with a prince, throwing a twig, a stone, water.
versions.text:
A king's son, in service to a giant, is set tasks he cannot do, and the giant's youngest daughter does them for him by magic. When the giant plans to kill him anyway, she cuts an apple into pieces that answer for them from the bed, and the two escape on the giant's filly.

The giant comes after them. She tells the prince to put his hand in the filly's ear. He finds a twig of sloe tree, and when he throws it behind them, it becomes twenty miles of blackthorn wood so thick a weasel could hardly get through. The giant goes home for his axe and cuts through it. Next the prince finds a splinter of grey stone in the filly's ear and throws it: twenty miles of rock. The giant fetches a pick and a mattock and breaks through. Last is a bladder of water. It becomes a fresh-water loch, and the giant, wading in after them, drowns.
sources: J. F. Campbell, Popular Tales of the West Highlands (1860), no. 2

image.caption: Illustration by John D. Batten for The Battle of the Birds in Joseph Jacobs, Celtic Fairy Tales, 1892

concepts.summary: Two minds meet and the loser forfeits a head, a kingdom or a life. A monster sets riddles at the city gate, a disguised god wagers his head with a giant, a young poet challenges an old one for the chair. Wisdom contests are common to oral cultures, and ritual versions, like the brahmodya exchanges of Vedic sacrifice, show how serious they could be. The endings rhyme across traditions, probably because they are the natural ways for such a contest to end: the challenger asks a question that cannot be answered from knowledge alone, a secret known only to himself, or receives an answer the questioner never expected.

versions.title: Samson's Riddle
versions.teaser: Out of the eater came something to eat.
versions.text:
On his way to his Philistine bride, Samson kills a young lion with his bare hands. Passing again, he finds a swarm of bees and honey in its carcass, scoops some out, and eats it as he walks. At the wedding feast he poses a riddle to the thirty young men assigned as his companions, betting thirty linen garments and thirty festal robes: 'Out of the eater came something to eat; out of the strong came something sweet.'

For three days they cannot solve it. They threaten his bride, and she weeps at him until, on the seventh day, he tells her. Before sunset the men answer: 'What is sweeter than honey? What is stronger than a lion?' Samson replies with a second riddle, sharper than the first: 'If you had not ploughed with my heifer, you would not have found out my riddle.' He pays the debt by killing thirty Philistines in Ashkelon and taking their clothes.

versions.title: Yōišt and the Sorcerer
versions.teaser: A young man answers a wizard's riddles and asks one he cannot answer.
versions.text:
The Avesta mentions it briefly: Yōišta of the Friyāna family sacrifices to the goddess Anāhitā and asks for the strength to overcome the wicked Akhtya and answer his hard riddles. The Pahlavi text named after him tells the story in full.

The sorcerer Axt arrives at the city of the riddle-solvers with a great army and announces that he will ask his questions of whoever will answer, and kill whoever fails. Many have already died. The young Yōišt comes forward and answers every question the sorcerer can devise. Then it is his turn. He asks Axt three questions, and the sorcerer, for all his learning, cannot answer them. Yōišt kills him. The questioner who has turned wisdom into a weapon is undone by the first person willing to question him back.
versions.caveat: The Avestan reference is only a few lines; the narrative is known from a Pahlavi text of the Islamic period.

versions.title: The Riddle of the Sphinx
versions.teaser: A monster outside Thebes asks what walks on four, then two, then three.
versions.text:
Hera sends the Sphinx to Thebes: a creature with the face of a woman, the body of a lion and the wings of a bird. She sits on Mount Phicium and puts to passing Thebans a riddle she learned from the Muses: what is it that has one voice and becomes four-footed, two-footed and three-footed? Whoever cannot answer, she seizes and devours. The Thebans have an oracle that they will be rid of her when the riddle is solved, and they meet often to puzzle over it, losing one of their number each time.

Oedipus, arriving on the road from Delphi, answers: man, who crawls on four limbs as a baby, walks on two when grown, and leans on a staff in old age. The Sphinx throws herself from the citadel. Oedipus gets the throne of Thebes and the widowed queen. The man who could read every riddle cannot read his own story, which is the riddle Sophocles builds his tragedy on.

image.caption: Oedipus and the Sphinx, Jean-Auguste-Dominique Ingres, begun 1808 (Louvre)

versions.title: The Questions of the Yakṣa
versions.teaser: Four brothers lie dead by a lake; the eldest must answer.
versions.text:
In the forest, the thirsty Pāṇḍava brothers find a clear lake. A voice, speaking from a crane, warns each in turn not to drink until he has answered its questions. Each ignores it, drinks, and falls dead. At last Yudhiṣṭhira comes, sees his four brothers on the bank, and agrees to answer.

The spirit, a yakṣa, asks question after question. What is heavier than the earth? A mother. What is higher than the sky? A father. What is swifter than the wind? The mind. What is more numerous than grass? Thoughts. What is the greatest wonder? That day after day creatures go to the house of death, and those who remain still wish to live forever. Satisfied, the yakṣa offers to revive one brother. Yudhiṣṭhira chooses Nakula, his half-brother, so that each of his father's two wives may have a surviving son. The yakṣa reveals himself as Dharma, Yudhiṣṭhira's own father, and restores them all.

versions.title: The Colloquy of the Two Sages
versions.teaser: Two poets contest the chief ollam's chair in language no one else understands.
versions.text:
The chief poet of Ulster dies, and his office is given to Ferchertne. Néde, son of the dead poet, returning from his studies in Scotland, takes his father's chair, thinking no one will dispute it. Ferchertne arrives and asks who this young man is who sits in the seat of wisdom.

The contest that follows is a dialogue of questions and answers in dense, riddling poetic language. Where have you come from? Néde answers: from the heel of a sage, from a confluence of wisdom, from the perfection of goodness. What is your name? What art do you practise? The answers pile up in kennings, until Néde, recognising the greater master, kneels and yields the chair. The tale adds a sting. King Conchobar and his nobles could not understand a word of the dispute, and decided that the poets should no longer have sole right of judgement.
sources: Immacallam in Dá Thuarad (The Colloquy of the Two Sages)

versions.title: Odin and Vafþrúðnir
versions.teaser: The god wagers his head against a giant's on questions about the world.
versions.text:
Against Frigg's advice, Odin sets out to test the wisdom of the giant Vafþrúðnir. He arrives at the giant's hall calling himself Gagnráðr, and they agree that the loser forfeits his head. First the giant questions the guest standing on the floor: the names of the horses that draw day and night, the river that divides gods from giants, the field of the last battle. Gagnráðr answers everything and is invited to sit.

Then Odin asks: where earth and sky came from, where the wind comes from, who will survive Ragnarök, how Odin will die. The giant answers them all. Then comes the last question: what did Odin whisper in his son's ear before Baldr was carried to the pyre? No one could know that but Odin himself. Vafþrúðnir recognises his guest, admits that he spoke his own doom with a doomed mouth, and concedes that Odin will always be the wisest.

versions.title: Gestumblindi's Riddles
versions.teaser: A disguised guest outwits a riddling king, and flies away as a falcon.
versions.text:
King Heiðrekr has sworn that any man who offends him may win his life by posing a riddle the king cannot solve. A man named Gestumblindi is summoned for judgement, and Odin comes to the court in his shape. He poses riddle after riddle, and Heiðrekr answers each: ale, the waves, which are the daughters of Ægir, a mother duck nesting in an ox's skull.

At last the guest asks the question that won the contest against Vafþrúðnir: what did Odin say in Baldr's ear before he was put on the pyre? Heiðrekr knows at once who his guest is. He draws the sword Tyrfingr and strikes at him, but Odin turns into a falcon and escapes through the roof, and the blade clips his tail feathers. That, the saga says, is why the falcon's tail is short. Odin curses the king to be killed by the worst of slaves, and so he is.

versions.title: Väinämöinen and Joukahainen
versions.teaser: A boastful young singer challenges the old sage and sinks into a swamp.
versions.text:
Young Joukahainen, jealous of Väinämöinen's fame, drives his sleigh straight into the old singer's on the road and refuses to give way. He demands a contest of knowledge. He knows, he says, that the titmouse lives in a tree and the pike spawns in the cold season, that the ploughing was done by gods and the sea dug out by them. Väinämöinen dismisses this as a child's learning, a woman's memory. Joukahainen claims then to have been present at the creation, helping to lay out the world.

That is a lie too far. Väinämöinen begins to sing, and the ground shakes. He sings Joukahainen's sword into lightning, his bow into a rainbow, his horse into a rock, and Joukahainen himself into a swamp, up to his waist, then his armpits, then his mouth. In desperation the young man offers his sister Aino as a wife. Väinämöinen accepts, sings him free, and starts the Kalevala's first tragedy.
versions.caveat: This is a contest of knowledge and magical song rather than riddles in the strict sense.
